title: Large language models, what they are and how they are trained

items.context: At its core, what does an LLM do?
items.why:
It gives a probability for every possible next token; one is picked and appended, and the
model runs again. Chat, summaries and code all come from this one loop.
items.true: Gives a probability for the next token, then repeats
false: Looks up the answer in a database of facts
Searches the web and summarizes what it finds
Runs a program written for each kind of question

items.context: How does a chatbot turn your question into an answer?
items.why:
The app wraps your message in a script, with special tokens marking who speaks. The model
continues that script one token at a time, and the app shows only the reply.
items.true: It continues a hidden script that holds your message
false: It retrieves a stored answer that matches your question
It writes the whole answer at once, then checks it
It turns your question into a database query

items.context:
Lecture 16's generative models drew a whole point (x, y) at once. How does an LLM generate
a text?
items.why:
A text has far too many possible values to draw at once. One token at a time, each step is
one choice from the vocabulary, and the chain rule makes the result exact.
items.true: One token at a time, each given the tokens before it
false: Every token at once, like one sample from a Gaussian mixture
Word by word, with each word drawn independently
As one whole sentence, picked from a list of candidates

items.context: Why is predicting the next token enough to model a whole text?
items.why:
The probability of a text is exactly the product of its next-token probabilities, with no
approximation. Learn those, and the model can both score a text and write one.
items.true: The chain rule splits p(text) into next-token probabilities
false: Each word depends only on the word right before it
It is a rough approximation that works for short texts
The model memorizes every text it was trained on

items.context:
An LLM writing an answer works like Lecture 8's recursive forecast. What weakness do they
share?
items.why:
Both use their own predictions as later inputs. In Lecture 8 the forecast drifted to the
mean; in an LLM, one wrong token early on steers the rest of the answer.
items.true: Each output is fed back in, so early errors carry forward
false: Both can look back only a fixed 10 steps
Both are linear models of their inputs
Both must be trained on labels written by people

items.why:
The tokenizer cuts text into tokens and gives each one a number, its id. The model never
sees letters, only the ids.
items.true: A piece of text: a character, a word or part of a word
false: One full sentence of the prompt
One parameter of the model
One layer of the transformer

items.context: Byte-pair encoding merges frequent pieces of text into single tokens. What does that buy?
items.why:
Frequent pieces become one token, so sequences get shorter: more text fits in the context
window and generation takes fewer steps. Rare words still split into known pieces.
items.true: Fewer tokens per text: more fits, and writing is faster
false: Exactly one token for every word ever written
A model that no longer needs a vocabulary
Rare words are dropped, so the text gets cleaner

items.context:
An LLM reads "4140" as two text pieces, "414" and "0". What should you do with arithmetic
and unit conversions?
items.why:
The model predicts digits as text; it does not calculate. Numbers, units and part numbers
are where LLMs slip, so check them and compute in code.
items.true: Do them in code, not in the model
false: Write every number in scientific notation
Raise the temperature so it tries more digits
Nothing: the model computes them exactly

items.context:
You paste a manual longer than the model's context window. What happens to the part past
the window?
items.why:
The context window is the most tokens the model can take in at once. Text beyond it is not
part of the input, so long documents must be cut, summarized or searched first.
false: It is read, but with lower attention weights
It is summarized automatically before answering
It is stored and read on your next question

items.context: What happens in one training step of an LLM?
items.why:
Show it text, let it guess each next token, compare with the token that really came next,
and take a gradient step on every parameter. Repeat, many times over.
items.true: It guesses next tokens; all parameters are nudged toward the truth
false: A person corrects its answers and rewrites its rules
It saves the text in a database to look up when asked later
It picks the best of several models trained side by side

items.context: Pretraining uses trillions of tokens that nobody labeled. Where do the targets come from?
items.why:
The target at every position is the token that actually came next. That is why any text
can be used, without anyone labeling it.
items.true: The text itself, shifted by one token
false: People who label a small sample of it
A smaller model that labels it first
The tokenizer, which marks tokens right or wrong

items.context: An LLM uses Lecture 12's transformer with one change. Which?
items.why:
A causal mask hides later tokens. In training the next token is the answer, so it has to
stay hidden.
items.true: Each token sees only itself and earlier tokens
false: There is no attention, only the MLP
Each token sees only the token right before it
The tokens are read from right to left

items.context:
Trained on our notes alone, the tiny GPT spells our terms but writes no meaningful sentence.
What would help most?
items.why:
It already copies our style. Meaning takes far more data and parameters; training longer
on the same small text only memorizes it.
items.true: Far more text, and a bigger model
false: Training longer on the same notes
A higher sampling temperature
A longer context window

items.context:
A pretrained model continues your question instead of answering it. What turns it into a
chat model?
items.why:
Supervised fine-tuning trains on examples of good answers; RLHF or DPO then trains on which
of two answers people prefer. More pretraining only makes it better at continuing text.
items.true: More training on good answers and on people's preferences
false: More pretraining on web text
A larger context window
A lower temperature

items.context: You ask an LLM about last week's measurements from your plant. What is the problem?
items.why:
Training stops at a cutoff date and never sees your company's documents. Put the data it
needs in the prompt, and do not ask it for current values.
items.true: It knows only its training data: nothing recent or private
false: Measurements are too numeric for any LLM to read
It refuses every question about a specific plant
A week of data is always too long for its context window

items.context: You lower the temperature. What happens to the text the model writes?
items.why:
Low temperature sharpens the probabilities toward the most likely token. High temperature
flattens them, so the text gets more varied and makes more mistakes.
items.true: Safer and more repetitive: it sticks to the likeliest tokens
false: More varied: unlikely tokens get a real chance
Nothing changes; only the speed goes up
It switches to a smaller vocabulary

items.context: Why can an LLM state a wrong number as fluently as a right one?
items.why:
Pretraining makes likely text likely, true or not. That is why every number and unit from
an LLM has to be checked against a measurement, a handbook or a calculation.
items.true: Training rewards likely text; nothing checks facts
false: Numbers are hidden from the model during training
A low temperature forces it to guess
It was trained on simulated data only

items.context:
The same prompt can give a different answer, even at temperature 0. As in Lecture 1, what
should you save?
items.why:
Providers do not promise identical outputs for identical inputs. A result you cannot
regenerate has to be stored, with what produced it: Lecture 1's reproducibility rule.
items.true: The output you used, with the model's name and the date
false: Only the prompt; the output can always be regenerated
The temperature setting, which fixes the output
Nothing: rerun the prompt when you need it
